source_refs.note: Book p. 56-57: 4.4.3 Properties of Determinants i-viii, Note on triangular matrices, Example 6; callouts marked Teaching note / Key points / Common mistake are ours.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Expanding a determinant of order 3 takes time and invites sign errors. The properties below let us simplify a determinant first, or even find its value without expanding it. In the list, \(R_{1}, R_{2}, R_{3}\) stand for rows and \(C_{1}, C_{2}, C_{3}\) for columns.

items: ii. If in a square matrix \(A\), two rows or two columns are interchanged, the determinant of the resulting matrix is \(-|A|\).
iii. If a square matrix \(A\) has two identical rows or two identical columns, then \(|A| = 0\).
iv. If all the entries of a row (or a column) of a square matrix \(A\) are zero, then \(|A| = 0\).
v. If the entries of a row (or a column) in a square matrix \(A\) are multiplied by a number \(k \in \mathbb{R}\), then the determinant of the resulting matrix is \(k|A|\).
vi. If each entry of a row (or a column) of a square matrix consists of two terms, then its determinant can be written as the sum of two determinants (see below).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints the equation of property vi twice: once with \(|B| =\) in front and once more, directly below, without it. The second line is a repetition; the property needs the equation only once.

items: vii. If any row (column) of a determinant is multiplied by a non-zero number \(k\) and the result is added to the corresponding entries of another row (column), the value of the determinant does not change.
viii. If a matrix is in triangular form, then the value of its determinant is the product of the entries on its main diagonal.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: We shall define triangular matrices on following pages.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why do these hold? Most follow from expansion. For example, iv: expand along the zero row and every term has a factor 0. iii: interchanging the two identical rows changes nothing, yet by ii it changes the sign, so \(|A| = -|A|\), which forces \(|A| = 0\). v: expand along the multiplied row and \(k\) comes out of every term.
Two uses of v: a common factor of a row or column can be taken outside the determinant, and a determinant with one row a multiple of another is 0 (take the factor out, then two rows are identical).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Our own illustration (not from the book). For
\[P = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 5 & 6 \\ 7 & 8 & 10 \end{bmatrix}\]
we get \(|P| = 1(50 - 48) - 2(40 - 42) + 3(32 - 35) = 2 + 4 - 9 = -3\). Then:
i. \(|P^{t}| = -3\) (same value).
ii. Interchange \(R_{1}\) and \(R_{2}\): the value becomes \(3\).
v. Multiply \(R_{1}\) by 2: the value becomes \(-6\).
vii. \(R_{2} - 4R_{1} \to R_{2}\) gives rows \(1, 2, 3\); \(0, -3, -6\); \(7, 8, 10\): the value is still \(-3\).
viii. A triangular example: \(\begin{vmatrix} 2 & 5 & 7 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \end{vmatrix} = 2 \times 3 \times 4 = 24\).

blocks.title: Example 6
blocks.problem: Without expansion, show that \(\begin{vmatrix} x & a+x & b+c \\ x & b+x & c+a \\ x & c+x & a+b \end{vmatrix} = 0\)
steps:
Given: the determinant
\[\begin{vmatrix} x & a+x & b+c \\ x & b+x & c+a \\ x & c+x & a+b \end{vmatrix}\]
To prove: its value is 0, without expanding it.
Method: use the properties. If we can make two columns identical, property iii gives 0 at once. Adding \(C_{3}\) to \(C_{2}\) (property vii) makes every entry of \(C_{2}\) equal to \(a + b + c + x\).

Step 1: Add the entries of \(C_{3}\) to the corresponding entries of \(C_{2}\)
\[= \begin{vmatrix} x & a+b+c+x & b+c \\ x & a+b+c+x & c+a \\ x & a+b+c+x & a+b \end{vmatrix}\]
Why: \((a + x) + (b + c)\), \((b + x) + (c + a)\) and \((c + x) + (a + b)\) all equal \(a + b + c + x\). By property vii (with \(k = 1\)) this does not change the value.

Step 2: Take common factors out of \(C_{1}\) and \(C_{2}\)
\[= x(a+b+c+x)\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & b+c \\ 1 & 1 & c+a \\ 1 & 1 & a+b \end{vmatrix}\]
Why: \(x\) is common to all of \(C_{1}\), and \(a + b + c + x\) is common to all of \(C_{2}\). By property v a common factor of one column comes outside the determinant.

Step 3: Two identical columns
\[= x(a+b+c+x) \cdot 0\]
\[= 0\]
Why: now \(C_{1}\) and \(C_{2}\) are identical (both \(1, 1, 1\)), so the determinant is 0 by property iii.

Check:
Expanding fully (which the question did not ask for) gives the same: each of the six products of formula (vii) cancels with another, and a computer algebra check gives 0 for all \(a, b, c, x\). For example, with \(x = 1, a = 2, b = 3, c = 4\) the rows are \(1, 3, 7\); \(1, 4, 6\); \(1, 5, 5\), and
\[1(20 - 30) - 3(5 - 6) + 7(5 - 4)\]
\[= -10 + 3 + 7 = 0\]
blocks.answer: Hence proved: \(\begin{vmatrix} x & a+x & b+c \\ x & b+x & c+a \\ x & c+x & a+b \end{vmatrix} = 0\)

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Transposing: value unchanged. Interchanging two rows (columns): sign changes.
2. Two identical rows (columns), or a zero row (column): value 0.
3. A common factor of one row (column) comes outside: \(k|A|\).
4. Adding \(k\) times one row (column) to another: value unchanged. This is how zeros are created before expanding.
5. Triangular matrix: product of the main-diagonal entries.
6. "Without expansion" means: use these properties to reach two identical rows/columns or a zero row/column.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Taking \(k\) out of the whole matrix: \(|kA| = k^{3}|A|\) for order 3, not \(k|A|\). Property v is about ONE row or column.
2. Forgetting the sign change when interchanging two rows.
3. Changing the row being added to: in \(R_{2} + kR_{1} \to R_{2}\) only \(R_{2}\) changes; \(R_{1}\) stays as it was.
4. Splitting a determinant (property vi) in two rows at once: split one row or column at a time.
